back: Empirical: based on finished, working product. Surrogate: a stand-in such as percent done, which is a prediction.
Green on the outside, red on the inside: status looks fine until shortly before the deadline.
The rate at which the team produces, validates and accepts deliverables per interval. Usually story points completed per iteration.
A planning aid for the team that produced it. Not a performance target, and not comparable between teams.
Comparing or ranking teams; false precision (treating points as the same across teams); making it a target.
Work remaining versus the time left in a timebox. The line falls toward zero.
Work completed toward a milestone, rising toward a total-scope line across the top.

front: Which burn chart shows a scope change clearly?
back: The burnup chart: the total-scope line moves.

front: Burndown: actual line above the ideal line
back: More work remains than planned: the team is behind.

front: Burndown: actual line below the ideal line
back: Less work remains than planned: the team is ahead.
Nothing is being finished. Look for an impediment.
Quantitative measures such as throughput, work in process and cycle time that show how efficiently work items move through a process.
The number of work items finished per time period.
Elapsed time from when work on an item starts to when it is finished.
Elapsed time from the customer's request to delivery of a usable product or feature.
Lead time starts at the request; cycle time starts when work begins. Lead time = waiting time + cycle time.
The number of items being worked on at a moment. Limiting it exposes bottlenecks and reduces task switching.
Problems found after release. An indicator of product quality and of a sustainable pace.
The number of items waiting in each workflow state. Growing queues signal bottlenecks.
Stacked bands showing the number of items in each state over time. Reveals WIP, cycle time, throughput and bottlenecks.

front: CFD: a band that keeps widening
back: A bottleneck: work enters that state faster than it leaves.

front: CFD: vertical and horizontal distance between the arrival and done lines
back: Vertical: work in process. Horizontal: approximate cycle time.
Customer satisfaction or Net Promoter Score; business value delivered; adoption and usage; time to learn.
A visible, physical display that shares information with the organization. Also called a big visible chart or, in lean, a visual control.
Information radiators are often kept by hand, not generated by software, so they are easy to update.
Team members help finish the work that is slowing the flow before starting anything new.
Start small and evolve; visualize openly; review and act; drop low-value metrics.

front: How to forecast for a sponsor
back: As a range with a confidence level, based on throughput. Never as a single-point commitment.
A regularly occurring workshop in which the team explores its work and results to improve both the process and the product.
At least at the end of each iteration; also after a release, when a few weeks have passed, when work is stuck, or at a milestone.
Qualitative (people's feelings) and quantitative (measurements), used to find root causes and plan actions.

front: How many retrospective actions should the team take on?
back: Only as many as it has capacity to finish in the next period.
Retrospective: the process, team only. Demonstration: the product, with stakeholders.

front: Retrospective vs lessons learned at project end
back: A retrospective is held throughout the project, so improvements help this project, not only the next one.
Completed features (or points) ÷ planned features. 25 completed of 30 planned = 0.83.
Earned value (the value of completed features) ÷ actual cost.
The time an item waits until work starts. Also called reaction time.
Capacity: burnup and burndown charts. Predictability: lead time and cycle time.
Three lines: features complete, features remaining, total features. A rising total shows that requirements grew.

front: How long until velocity is stable?
back: It can take four to eight iterations.
